title: Randomised Work Stealing
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In work stealing, each processor keeps a deque of ready tasks and an idle processor steals from the opposite end of another processor's deque.
short: Thieves take old work; owners take new work.
long: Thieves take old work; owners take new work. Random victim choice gives good expected load balance with little communication.
proof: Classic randomized analyses bound the expected execution time in terms of total work T1 and critical-path length T-infinity.
consequence: Work stealing is used in Cilk, Java fork-join and many task runtimes.

title: Amdahl's Law for Speedup
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: If a fraction f of computation is inherently serial, the maximum speedup with p processors is at most 1/(f + (1-f)/p).
short: The serial fraction caps all speedup.
long: The serial fraction caps all speedup. As p grows the speedup approaches 1/f, no matter how many processors are added.
proof: Scaled time is fT + (1-f)T/p, so the ratio of original to scaled time gives the formula.
consequence: It warns that optimising only the parallel portion has diminishing returns.

title: Gustafson's Scaled Speedup
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: When problem size grows with the number of processors, scaled speedup can remain near-linear despite a fixed serial fraction.
short: Bigger machines tackle bigger problems.
long: Bigger machines tackle bigger problems. It offers a more optimistic complement to Amdahl's fixed-work view.
proof: Writing serial and parallel portions as fractions alpha and 1-alpha of the scaled run gives the linear expression.
consequence: It explains strong scaling results in scientific computing.

title: Race Conditions Break Determinism
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Two processes incrementing the same shared counter without synchronisation can lose updates, giving a nondeterministic result.
short: Read-modify-write needs mutual exclusion.
long: Read-modify-write needs mutual exclusion. The same program may produce different outputs on different schedules.
proof: Both processors can read the same old value before either writes, so one increment is lost.
consequence: Parallel algorithms must specify disjoint writes or use atomic operations and reductions.

title: Barrier Synchronization
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A barrier makes all participating threads wait until every thread reaches it before any proceeds.
short: A rendezvous point for parallel phases.
long: A rendezvous point for parallel phases. Tree and centralised barriers trade latency against contention; misuse can cause deadlock.
proof: No thread passes until the count of arrivals equals the number of participants.
consequence: Barriers separate phases in BSP and data-parallel loops.

title: Simulating PRAM on Interconnection Networks
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Any PRAM algorithm can be simulated on a suitably connected network with only a logarithmic slowdown using routing and hashing techniques.
short: Distributed memory need not lose much theoretical power.
long: Distributed memory need not lose much theoretical power. Constant-degree networks such as hypercubes and butterflies support such simulations.
proof: Emulate shared cells by distributing them across processors and routing each request in O(log p) steps.
consequence: PRAM bounds remain a useful first approximation on real networks.

title: Hypercube Network Diameter
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A d-dimensional hypercube with 2^d nodes has diameter d = log2 p, so any two processors communicate in at most log p routing steps.
short: Flip differing bits to route.
long: Flip differing bits to route. Each node has degree d, giving a good balance between connectivity and hardware cost.
proof: Flipping the differing bit positions one at a time transforms any node label into any other in Hamming distance steps.
consequence: Hypercubes were an early parallel-machine topology.

title: Butterfly Network Routing
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A butterfly network routes any input to any output through log p stages using bit-fixing routes.
short: Each stage fixes one address bit.
long: Each stage fixes one address bit. It supports efficient emulation of shared memory and fast Fourier-style communication patterns.
proof: At stage i, route straight or cross according to bit i of source and destination until all bits match.
consequence: Butterflies underpin many parallel routing and sorting architectures.

title: External Memory Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: The external memory model has a fast memory of M items and disk blocks of B items, counting only block transfers as I/Os.
short: Optimise disk transfers, not CPU instructions.
long: Optimise disk transfers, not CPU instructions. Sequential scans cost Theta(N/B) I/Os; random access may cost one I/O per access.
proof: The model is a definition: computation is free while each block transfer costs one I/O.
consequence: It explains why B-trees and merge sort dominate disk-based systems.

title: External Sorting Lower Bound
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Sorting N items in external memory requires Theta((N/B) log_{M/B}(N/B)) I/Os under the standard tall-cache assumption.
short: Merge logarithmically many runs of size M/B blocks.
long: Merge logarithmically many runs of size M/B blocks. The bound is the external analogue of the comparison-sort lower bound.
proof: Each merge pass reads and writes the whole dataset once, and the number of passes is logarithmic in N/M.
consequence: It sets the target for external and cache-oblivious sorting algorithms.

title: External Merge Sort with Run Merging
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: External merge sort reads chunks of M items, sorts them in memory into runs, then merges runs using one input buffer per run and one output buffer.
short: Sort in memory, merge sequentially on disk.
long: Sort in memory, merge sequentially on disk. Multiway merging reduces the number of passes compared with binary merging.
proof: Each merge pass scans each item once in and once out, giving O(N/B) I/Os per pass and O(log_{M/B}(N/B)) passes.
consequence: It is the standard algorithm for sorting data larger than RAM.

title: B-Tree Search I/O Bound
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A B-tree with fan-out Theta(B) searches N items in O(log_B N) block transfers.
short: Each level of the tree costs one disk read.
long: Each level of the tree costs one disk read. This is optimal for comparison-based external search.
proof: Each node fits in one block and has Theta(B) children, so height is logarithmic base B.
consequence: B-trees minimise disk I/O in database indexes.

title: Cache-Oblivious Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In the cache-oblivious model algorithms are written without knowing B or M yet achieve optimal I/O bounds on every block size.
short: Write once, optimal on every cache level.
long: Write once, optimal on every cache level. It uses an ideal fully associative cache with optimal replacement.
proof: Recursive divide-and-conquer layouts work across all scales, so no parameter tuning is needed.
consequence: A single algorithm can exploit an entire memory hierarchy automatically.

title: Cache-Oblivious Matrix Transpose
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Recursive quadrant-wise transposition achieves Theta(N^2/B) cache misses without knowing the block size.
short: Divide the matrix until blocks fit in cache.
long: Divide the matrix until blocks fit in cache. The recursion also respects multiple cache levels simultaneously.
proof: Once submatrices fit in cache the transfer is optimal; larger cases reduce to four recursive transposes.
consequence: It outperforms naive row-by-row transpose on large matrices.

title: Cache-Oblivious Sorting Bound
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Cache-oblivious sorting achieves O((N/B) log_{M/B}(N/B)) I/Os without knowing B or M.
short: Recursive distribution matches external merge sort.
long: Recursive distribution matches external merge sort. The funnelsort algorithm uses buffered merging to obtain the optimal bound.
proof: Recursive splitting until subproblems fit in cache, combined with buffer trees, yields the external-sort I/O bound at every level.
consequence: It gives one sorting routine optimal across all cache levels.

title: Cache-Oblivious B-Tree
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A cache-oblivious B-tree supports searches and updates in O(log_B N) I/Os without knowing B, using a static binary tree laid out in van Emde Boas order.
short: Recursive layout simulates high fan-out at every block size.
long: Recursive layout simulates high fan-out at every block size. Updates use buffered rebuilds to maintain the layout efficiently.
proof: The vEB layout groups subtrees of the right height into contiguous blocks, so each memory level sees an effective B-tree.
consequence: It delivers B-tree I/O performance with no tuning parameters.

title: Streaming Model One-Pass Constraint
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In the streaming model data arrives as a long sequence and the algorithm uses sublinear memory with one or few passes.
short: See each item once, remember little.
long: See each item once, remember little. Exact answers are often impossible, so approximations and sketches are standard.
proof: The model restricts both memory and pass count, forcing summarisation.
consequence: It models routers, sensor networks and clickstream analysis.

title: Turnstile Stream Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In a turnstile stream, items can be both inserted and deleted, so the underlying frequency vector receives positive and negative updates.
short: Frequencies can go down as well as up.
long: Frequencies can go down as well as up. Algorithms such as count-min sketches tolerate negative updates, while many heavy-hitters methods do not.
proof: The stream is modelled as a sequence of signed updates to a vector.
consequence: It captures network flows and dynamic multisets more realistically than insertion-only streams.

title: Reservoir Sampling Uniform Sample
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Keeping the j-th item with probability k/j replaces a uniformly chosen member of a size-k reservoir, yielding a uniform sample of any prefix of the stream.
short: Sample without knowing the stream length.
long: Sample without knowing the stream length. It uses one pass and O(k) memory.
proof: Induction: after j items each of them is in the reservoir with probability k/j.
consequence: It is the standard way to sample from huge or unknown-size datasets.

title: I/O Optimal Scanning and Hashing
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Sequential scans are optimal in external memory, taking Theta(N/B) I/Os, whereas hash-table lookups can cost one I/O each.
short: Batching random accesses into sequential ones pays off.
long: Batching random accesses into sequential ones pays off. External hash tables arrange buckets so that probes within a bucket are contiguous.
proof: A scan transfers each block once; random accesses may touch a different block per item.
consequence: Disk-based systems prefer log-structured and sorted layouts over pointer-heavy structures.

title: KMP Prefix Function Definition
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The prefix function pi[i] of a string is the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of s[0..i].
short: Each position remembers its longest border.
long: Each position remembers its longest border. The whole function is computed in O(m) time for a pattern of length m.
proof: If pi[i-1] = k, only borders of the prefix of length k need checking when extending by one character.
consequence: It is the core table of the Knuth–Morris–Pratt matcher.

title: KMP Linear-Time Pattern Matching
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Using the prefix function to shift the pattern after a mismatch finds all occurrences in a text of length n in O(n + m) time.
short: Mismatches redirect via previously computed borders.
long: Mismatches redirect via previously computed borders. The text pointer never moves backward, so the bound is worst-case rather than average-case.
proof: Each text character is compared O(1) times amortised because every mismatch follows a failure link to a strictly shorter border.
consequence: KMP avoids the quadratic behaviour of naive matching on repetitive texts.

title: KMP Failure Links Avoid Text Backtracking
subject: String Algorithms
statement: After a mismatch, KMP shifts the pattern so that its longest matching prefix aligns with the text suffix, without re-examining text characters.
short: Reuse what already matched.
long: Reuse what already matched. This is what distinguishes KMP from naive backtracking matchers.
proof: Any shorter shift would misalign characters already known to match at the suffix.
consequence: It gives predictable linear performance on adversarial inputs.

title: Z-Function Longest Common Prefixes
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The Z-value at position i is the length of the longest common prefix of the whole string and the suffix starting at i.
short: Z-values measure self-similarity at every shift.
long: Z-values measure self-similarity at every shift. Z[0] is usually defined as 0 or n by convention.
proof: The definition is a direct comparison of the string with each of its suffixes.
consequence: Z-values support linear-time pattern matching and periodicity tests.

title: Z-Algorithm Linear Construction
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Maintaining the rightmost matching Z-box lets all Z-values of a string be computed in O(n) time.
short: Reuse inside previously matched intervals.
long: Reuse inside previously matched intervals. Combining pattern, separator and text with Z-values gives another linear pattern matcher.
proof: Comparisons inside an existing box are copied, and each comparison extending the box increases its right boundary.
consequence: The Z-algorithm is a compact alternative to the prefix function.
